**Sir Vidiadhar Surajprasad Naipaul**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-1) (17 August 1932 – 11 August 2018) was a Trinidad-born British writer renowned for his works of fiction and nonfiction in English. He is known for his comic early novels set in Trinidad, his bleaker novels of alienation in the wider world, and his vigilant chronicles of life and travels. He wrote in prose that was widely admired, but his views sometimes aroused controversy. He published more than thirty books over fifty years.

Naipaul's breakthrough novel _[A House for Mr Biswas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_House\_for\_Mr\_Biswas "A House for Mr Biswas")_ was published in 1961. Naipaul won the Booker Prize in 1971 for his novel _[In a Free State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_a\_Free\_State "In a Free State")_.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-Booker_Prize_1971-2) He won the [Jerusalem Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerusalem_Prize "Jerusalem Prize") in 1983, and was awarded the [Trinity Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_Cross "Trinity Cross"), Trinidad and Tobago's highest national honour, in 1990. He received a [knighthood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Bachelor "Knight Bachelor") in 1990, and the [Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2001 Nobel Prize in Literature") in 2001.

## Life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life and career")]

### Background and early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Background and early life")]

> "Where there had been swamp at the foot of the [Northern Range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Range "Northern Range"), with mud huts with earthen walls that showed the damp halfway up ... there was now the landscape of Holland... Sugarcane as a crop had ceased to be important. None of the Indian villages were like villages I had known. No narrow roads; no dark, overhanging trees; no huts; no earth yards with hibiscus hedges; no ceremonial lighting of lamps, no play of shadows on the wall; no cooking of food in half-walled verandas, no leaping firelight; no flowers along gutters or ditches where frogs croaked the night away."[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1987352-3)

—From _Enigma of Arrival_ (1987)

V. S. Naipaul was born to Droapatie (_née_[Capildeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capildeo_family "Capildeo family")) and [Seepersad Naipaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seepersad_Naipaul "Seepersad Naipaul") on 17 August 1932 in the [sugar plantation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sugar_plantation "Sugar plantation")-town of [Chaguanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaguanas "Chaguanas") on the island of [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad"), the larger of the two islands in the British [crown colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_colony "Crown colony") of Trinidad and Tobago.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayward20025-4) He was the couple's second child and first son.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayward20025-4)

Naipaul's father, Seepersad, was an English-language journalist.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200818b-5) In 1929, he had begun contributing stories to the _[Trinidad Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad\_and\_Tobago\_Guardian "Trinidad and Tobago Guardian")_,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200819-6) and in 1932 he joined the staff as the provincial Chaguanas correspondent.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayward20027-7) In "A prologue to an autobiography" (1983), Naipaul describes how Seepersad's great reverence for writers and for the writing life spawned the dreams and aspirations of his eldest son.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200836%E2%80%9337-8)

In the 1880s, Naipaul's paternal grandfather had emigrated from [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") to work as an [indentured labourer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_indenture_system "Indian indenture system") in a sugar plantation.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200812-9) In the 1890s, his maternal grandfather was to do the same.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200812-9) During this time, many people in India, their prospects blighted by the [Great Famine of 1876–78](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Famine_of_1876%E2%80%9378 "Great Famine of 1876–78"), or similar calamities,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisariaVisaria1983515,a-10) had emigrated to distant outposts of the British Empire such as Trinidad and Tobago, [British Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Guiana "British Guiana"), [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Jamaica "Colony of Jamaica"), [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Fiji "Colony of Fiji"), [Mauritius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Mauritius "British Mauritius"), [Natal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Natal "Colony of Natal"), [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa_Protectorate "East Africa Protectorate"), [Malaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Malaya "British Malaya"), the French colonies of [Martinique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinique "Martinique") and [Guadeloupe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guadeloupe "Guadeloupe"), and the Dutch colony of [Suriname](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surinam_(Dutch_colony) "Surinam (Dutch colony)").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEVisariaVisaria1983515,b-11) Although slavery had been [abolished](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_Abolition_Act_1833 "Slavery Abolition Act 1833") in these places in 1833, slave labour was still in demand, and [indenture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indenture "Indenture") was the legal contract being drawn to meet the demand.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEHayward20025-4)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench20085-12)

According to the genealogy the Naipauls had reconstructed in Trinidad, they were [Hindu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu "Hindu")[Brahmins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmin "Brahmin")—embraced from the knowledge of his mother's family; his father's background had remained less certain.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200823%E2%80%9325-13) Their ancestors in India had been guided by ritual restrictions. Among these were those on food—including the prohibition against eating flesh—drink, attire and social interaction.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200855a-14)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/16/Trinidad_and_Tobago_Shaded_Relief_PCL_Texas_Annotated.jpg/250px-Trinidad_and_Tobago_Shaded_Relief_PCL_Texas_Annotated.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Trinidad_and_Tobago_Shaded_Relief_PCL_Texas_Annotated.jpg)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Indian_Women_go_Shopping_in_Port_of_Spain%2C_Trinidad%2C_1945%2C_National_Archives%2C_UK.jpg/250px-Indian_Women_go_Shopping_in_Port_of_Spain%2C_Trinidad%2C_1945%2C_National_Archives%2C_UK.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Indian_Women_go_Shopping_in_Port_of_Spain,_Trinidad,_1945,_National_Archives,_UK.jpg)

(Left) [Chaguanas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaguanas "Chaguanas") is just inward of the [Gulf of Paria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Paria "Gulf of Paria") coast. [County Caroni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroni_County "Caroni County") and [Naparima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naparima_Plain "Naparima Plain") were fictionalised as _County Naparoni_ in Naipaul's _[The Suffrage of Elvira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Suffrage\_of\_Elvira "The Suffrage of Elvira")_. (Right) Indian women go shopping in [Port-of-Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port-of-Spain "Port-of-Spain"), [Trinidad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinidad "Trinidad"), 1945.

In Trinidad, the restrictions were to gradually loosen. By the time of Naipaul's earliest childhood memories, chicken and fish were eaten at the family's dining table, and [Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christmas "Christmas") was celebrated with a dinner.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200855b-15) The men wore only western clothes. The women's [saris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sari "Sari") were being accessorised with belts and heeled footwear, their [hemlines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemline "Hemline") rising in imitation of the [skirt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skirt "Skirt"), and they were soon to disappear altogether as an item of daily wear.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008208%E2%80%93209-16) Disappearing as well were the languages of [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India"). Naipaul and his siblings were encouraged to speak only [English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200826-17) At school, other languages were taught, but these were usually [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language "Spanish language") and [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200841-18)

Naipaul's family moved to Trinidad's capital [Port of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Spain "Port of Spain"), at first when he was seven,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200830-19) and then more permanently when he was nine.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200832%E2%80%9333-20)

Naipaul was enrolled in the government-run [Queen's Royal College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Royal_College "Queen's Royal College") (QRC), an urban, cosmopolitan, high-performing school, which was designed and functioned in the fashion of a British boys' [public school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_school_(United_Kingdom) "Public school (United Kingdom)").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200840%E2%80%9341-21) Before he turned 17, he won a Trinidad Government scholarship to study abroad. He reflected later that the scholarship would have allowed him to study any subject at any institution of higher learning in the [British Commonwealth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Commonwealth "British Commonwealth"), but that he chose to go to [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") to do a degree in English. He went, he wrote, "in order at last to write...." In August 1950, Naipaul boarded a [Pan Am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_American_World_Airways "Pan American World Airways") flight to New York, continuing the next day by boat to London.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200867-22) He left Trinidad, like the narrator of _[Miguel Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel\_Street "Miguel Street")_, hardening himself to the emotion displayed by his family.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200867-22) For recording the impressions of his journey, Naipaul purchased a pad of paper and a [copying pencil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copying_pencil "Copying pencil"), noting, "I had bought the pad and pencil because I was travelling to become a writer, and I had to start."[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200867-22) The copious notes and letters from that time were to become the basis for the chapter "Journey" in Naipaul's novel _[The Enigma of Arrival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Enigma\_of\_Arrival "The Enigma of Arrival")_, written 37 years later.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200867-22)

Arriving at Oxford for the [Michaelmas term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaelmas_term "Michaelmas term"), 1950, Naipaul judged himself adequately prepared for his studies;[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200873a-23) in the judgement of his Latin tutor, [Peter Bayley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Bayley_(literary_critic) "Peter Bayley (literary critic)"), Naipaul showed promise and poise.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200873b-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200896-25) But, a year later, in Naipaul's estimation, his attempts at writing felt contrived. Unsure of his ability and calling, and lonely, he became depressed.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200890-26) By late March 1952, plans were made for his return to Trinidad in the summer.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200891-27) His father put down a quarter of the passage.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200891-27) However, in early April, in the _[vacs](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/vac "wiktionary:vac")_ before the [Trinity term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trinity_term "Trinity term"), Naipaul took an impulsive trip to Spain, and quickly spent all he had saved.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200892%E2%80%9393-28) Attempting an explanation to his family, he called it "a nervous breakdown".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench200893-29) Thirty years later, he was to call it "something like a mental illness."[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJussawalla1997126-30)

Earlier in 1952, at a college play, Naipaul had met Patricia Ann Hale, a history student. Hale and Naipaul formed a close friendship, which eventually developed into a sexual relationship. With Hale's support, Naipaul began to recover and gradually to write. In turn, she became a partner in planning his career. When they told their families about their relationship, the response was unenthusiastic; from her family it was hostile. In June 1953, both Naipaul and Hale graduated, both receiving, in his words, "a damn, bloody, ... [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_class_honours#Second-class_honours "Second class honours")."[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008115-31)[J. R. R. Tolkien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._R._R._Tolkien "J. R. R. Tolkien"), professor of [Anglo-Saxon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English") at [Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxford "Oxford"), however, judged Naipaul's Anglo-Saxon paper to have been the best in the university.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008115-31)

In Trinidad, Naipaul's father had had a [coronary thrombosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coronary_thrombosis "Coronary thrombosis") in early 1953,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008111-32) and lost his job at the _Guardian_ in the summer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008118-33) In October 1953, Seepersad Naipaul died.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008123-34) By [Hindu tenets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samskara_(rite_of_passage) "Samskara (rite of passage)"), it fell to Naipaul to light the funeral pyre—it was the mandatory ritual of the eldest son. But since there was not the time nor the money for Naipaul to return, his eight-year-old brother, [Shiva Naipaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva_Naipaul "Shiva Naipaul"), performed the final rites of cremation. "The event marked him," Naipaul wrote about his brother. "That death and cremation were his private wound."[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1987346-35)

Through the summer and autumn of 1953, Naipaul was financially depleted. His prospects for employment in frugal post-war Britain were unpromising, his applications to jobs overseas repeatedly rejected, and his attempts at writing as yet haphazard.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008117%E2%80%93128-36) Working off and on at odd jobs, borrowing money from Pat or his family in Trinidad, Naipaul reluctantly enrolled for a [B. Litt.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Letters "Bachelor of Letters") post-graduate degree at Oxford in [English Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Literature "English Literature").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008117%E2%80%93128-36) In December 1953, he failed his first B.Litt. exam.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008117%E2%80%93128-36) Although he passed the second written examination, his [viva voce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oral_exam "Oral exam"), in February 1954, with [F. P. Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/F._P._Wilson "F. P. Wilson"), an [Elizabethan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabethan_literature "Elizabethan literature") scholar and [Merton Professor of English Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merton_Professors "Merton Professors") at Oxford, did not go well. He was failed overall for the B.Litt. degree.[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-38) With that also ended all hopes of being supported for academic studies at Oxford.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008128-39) Naipaul would later say that he 'hated Oxford'.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTERosenTejpal1998-40)

### 1954–1956: London, _Caribbean Voices_, marriage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 1954–1956: London, Caribbean Voices, marriage")]

*   [![Image 9: Pauline Henriques and Samuel Selvon reading a story on BBC's Caribbean Voices. In December 1954, Naipaul joined the staff.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f6/Pauline_Henriques_Sam_Selvon_Caribbean_Voices_1952.jpg/250px-Pauline_Henriques_Sam_Selvon_Caribbean_Voices_1952.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pauline_Henriques_Sam_Selvon_Caribbean_Voices_1952.jpg "Pauline Henriques and Samuel Selvon reading a story on BBC's Caribbean Voices.  In December 1954, Naipaul joined the staff.") [Pauline Henriques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pauline_Henriques "Pauline Henriques") and [Samuel Selvon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Selvon "Samuel Selvon") reading a story on [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Broadcasting_Corporation "British Broadcasting Corporation")'s _[Caribbean Voices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean\_Voices "Caribbean Voices")_. In December 1954, Naipaul joined the staff. 
*   [![Image 10: The old Langham Hotel in a picture-postcard ca. 1903. Here, in 1955 in the BBC freelancers' room, Naipaul wrote the first story of Miguel Street.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/21/Langham_Hotel_London_post_card_1903.JPG/250px-Langham_Hotel_London_post_card_1903.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Langham_Hotel_London_post_card_1903.JPG "The old Langham Hotel in a picture-postcard ca. 1903. Here, in 1955 in the BBC freelancers' room, Naipaul wrote the first story of Miguel Street.") The old [Langham Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langham_Hotel,_London "Langham Hotel, London") in a picture-postcard ca. 1903. Here, in 1955 in the BBC freelancers' room, Naipaul wrote the first story of _[Miguel Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel\_Street "Miguel Street")_. 

> "The freelancers' room was like a club: chat, movement, the separate anxieties of young or youngish men below the passing fellowship of the room. That was the atmosphere I was writing in. That was the atmosphere I gave to Bogart's Port of Spain street. Partly for the sake of speed, and partly because my memory or imagination couldn't rise to it, I had given his servant room hardly any furniture: the Langham room itself was barely furnished. And I benefited from the fellowship of the room that afternoon. Without that fellowship, without the response of the three men who read the story, I might not have wanted to go on with what I had begun."

—From, "A Prologue to an Autobiography" (1983).[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1983c-41)

Naipaul moved to London, where he reluctantly accepted shelter in the flat of a cousin. Pat, who had won a scholarship for further studies at the University of Birmingham, moved out of her parents' flat to independent lodgings where Naipaul could visit her. For the remainder of 1954, Naipaul exhibited behaviour that tried the patience of those closest to him. He denounced Trinidad and Trinidadians; he castigated the British who he felt had taken him out of Trinidad but left him without opportunity; he took refuge in illness, but when help was offered, he rebuffed it. He was increasingly dependent on Pat, who remained loyal, offering him money, practical advice, encouragement, and rebuke.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-42)

Gainful employment appeared for Naipaul in December 1954. [Henry Swanzy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Swanzy "Henry Swanzy"), producer of the BBC weekly programme, _[Caribbean Voices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean\_Voices "Caribbean Voices")_, offered Naipaul a three-month renewable contract as presenter of the programme. Swanzy, on whose program a generation of Caribbean writers had debuted, including [George Lamming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Lamming "George Lamming"), [Samuel Selvon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Selvon "Samuel Selvon"), the 19-year-old [Derek Walcott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derek_Walcott "Derek Walcott") and, earlier, Naipaul himself, was being transferred to [Accra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accra "Accra") to manage the [Gold Coast Broadcasting System](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_Coast_Broadcasting_System "Gold Coast Broadcasting System"). Naipaul would stay in the part-time job for four years, and Pat would remain the critical breadwinner for the couple.

In January 1955, Naipaul moved to new lodgings, a small flat in [Kilburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilburn,_London "Kilburn, London"), and he and Pat were married. Neither informed their families or friends—their wedding guests were limited to the two witnesses required by law. Pat continued to live in Birmingham but visited on the weekends. At the BBC, Naipaul presented the programme once a week, wrote short reviews and conducted interviews. The sparsely furnished freelancers' room in the old [Langham Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langham_Hotel,_London "Langham Hotel, London") flowed with the banter of Caribbean writers and would-be writers, providing camaraderie and fellowship. There, one afternoon in the summer of 1955, Naipaul typed out a 3,000-word story. It was based on the memory of a neighbour he had known as a child in a [Port of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Spain "Port of Spain") street, but it also drew on the mood and ambience of the freelancers' room. Three fellow writers, John Stockbridge, [Andrew Salkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Salkey "Andrew Salkey"), and Gordon Woolford, who read the story later, were affected by it and encouraged him to go on. Over the next five weeks, Naipaul would write his first publishable book, _[Miguel Street](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miguel\_Street "Miguel Street")_, a collection of linked stories of that Port of Spain street. Although the book was not published right away, Naipaul's talent caught the attention of publishers and his spirits began to lift.

### 1956–1958: Early Trinidad novels

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 1956–1958: Early Trinidad novels")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/HMS-Cavina-WW2-1941-requisitioned-Elder%26Fyffes-Banana-Boat.jpg/250px-HMS-Cavina-WW2-1941-requisitioned-Elder%26Fyffes-Banana-Boat.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:HMS-Cavina-WW2-1941-requisitioned-Elder&Fyffes-Banana-Boat.jpg)

[HMS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her_Majesty's_Ship "Her Majesty's Ship")_Cavina_, the peacetime [Elders & Fyffes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyffes_Line "Fyffes Line") passenger-carrying [banana boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana_boat_(ship) "Banana boat (ship)"), shown in 1941, requisitioned for [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In August 1956, Naipaul returned on [TSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_turbine#Marine_propulsion "Steam turbine") Cavina to Trinidad for a two-month stay with his family.

[Diana Athill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diana_Athill "Diana Athill"), the editor at the publishing company André Deutsch, who read _Miguel Street_, liked it. But the publisher, [André Deutsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Deutsch "André Deutsch"), thought a series of linked stories by an unknown Caribbean writer unlikely to sell profitably in Britain.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008155%E2%80%93156-43) He encouraged Naipaul to write a novel.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008155%E2%80%93156-43) Without enthusiasm, Naipaul quickly wrote _[The Mystic Masseur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Mystic\_Masseur "The Mystic Masseur")_ in autumn 1955.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008155%E2%80%93156-43) On 8 December 1955, his novel was accepted by Deutsch, and Naipaul received a [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_sterling "Pound sterling")125 payment.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008155%E2%80%93156-43)

In late August 1956, six years after arriving in England, three years after his father's death, and in the face of pressure from his family in Trinidad, especially his mother, to visit, Naipaul boarded [TSS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_turbine#Marine_propulsion "Steam turbine")_Cavina_, an [Elders & Fyffes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyffes_Line "Fyffes Line") passenger-carrying [banana boat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banana_boat_(ship) "Banana boat (ship)"), in [Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol "Bristol").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008160-44) From on board the ship, he sent harsh and humorous descriptions of the ship's [West Indians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies") passengers to Pat, recording also their conversations in dialect.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008161-45) His early letters from Trinidad spoke to the wealth created there during the intervening years, in contrast to the prevailing frugal economy in Britain.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008163-46) Trinidad was in its last phase before decolonisation, and there was a new-found confidence among its citizens.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008164%E2%80%93165-47) Among Trinidad's different racial groups, there were also avowals of racial separateness—in contrast to the fluid, open racial attitudes of Naipaul's childhood—and there was violence.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008165-48) In the elections of 1956, the party supported by the majority blacks and Indian Muslims narrowly won, leading to an increased sense of gloom in Naipaul.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008167%E2%80%93168-49) Naipaul accompanied a politician uncle, a candidate of the Hindu party, to his campaign rallies.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008171%E2%80%93172-50) During these and other events he was gathering ideas for later literary use.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008171%E2%80%93172-50) By the time he left Trinidad, he had written to Pat about plans for a new novelette on a rural election in Trinidad.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008171%E2%80%93172-50) These would transmute upon his return to England into the comic novel _[The Suffrage of Elvira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Suffrage\_of\_Elvira "The Suffrage of Elvira")_.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008171%E2%80%93172-50)

Back in England, Deutsch informed Naipaul that _The Mystic Masseur_ would not be published for another ten months. Naipaul's anger at the publisher together with his anxiety about surviving as a writer aroused more creative energy: _The Suffrage of Elvira_ was written with great speed during the early months of 1957.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008173-51) In June 1957, _The Mystic Masseur_ was finally published. The reviews were generally complimentary, though some were also patronising. Still shy of his 25th birthday, Naipaul copied out many of the reviews by hand for his mother, including the _Daily Telegraph_'s, "V. S. Naipaul is a young writer who contrives to blend Oxford wit with home-grown rambunctiousness and not do harm to either."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008174%E2%80%93175-52) Awaiting his book royalties, in summer 1957, Naipaul accepted his only full-time employment, the position of editorial assistant at the Cement and Concrete Association (C&CA). The association published the magazine _Concrete Quarterly_.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008180%E2%80%93181-53) Although he disliked the desk job and remained in it for a mere ten weeks, the salary of £1,000 a year provided financial stability, allowing him to send money to Trinidad.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008180%E2%80%93181-53) The C&CA was also to be the office setting for Naipaul's later novel, _Mr Stone and the Knights Companion_.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008180%E2%80%93181-53) Around this same time, writer [Francis Wyndham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Wyndham_(Writer) "Francis Wyndham (Writer)"), who had taken Naipaul under his wing, introduced him to novelist [Anthony Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Powell "Anthony Powell"). Powell, in turn, convinced the publisher of the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_, [Kingsley Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsley_Martin "Kingsley Martin"), to give Naipaul a part-time job reviewing books.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008186%E2%80%93187-54) Naipaul would review books once a month from 1957 to 1961.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008186%E2%80%93187-54)

With many West Indian writers now active in England, _Caribbean Voices_ was judged to have achieved its purpose and slated to terminate in August 1958.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008179-55) Naipaul's relations with his BBC employers began to fray. Despite three years of hosting the programme and three completed novels, he had been unable to make the transition to mainstream BBC programming. He claimed later that he was told those jobs were reserved for Europeans.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008178%E2%80%93179-56) In July 1958, after arriving late for a program, Naipaul was reprimanded by the producers, and, in his words, "broke with the BBC".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008179%E2%80%93180-57)

With promotional help from [André Deutsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Deutsch "André Deutsch"), Naipaul's novels would soon receive critical acclaim.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008185-58)_The Mystic Masseur_ was awarded the [John Llewellyn Rhys Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Llewellyn_Rhys_Prize "John Llewellyn Rhys Prize") in 1958, and _Miguel Street_ the [Somerset Maugham Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somerset_Maugham_Award "Somerset Maugham Award") in 1961, [W. Somerset Maugham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W._Somerset_Maugham "W. Somerset Maugham") himself approving the first-ever selection of a non-European.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008185-58)

### 1957–1960: _A House for Mr Biswas_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 1957–1960: A House for Mr Biswas")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/0/0a/Seepersad_Naipaul_with_Ford_Prefect.jpg/250px-Seepersad_Naipaul_with_Ford_Prefect.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seepersad_Naipaul_with_Ford_Prefect.jpg)

[Seepersad Naipaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seepersad_Naipaul "Seepersad Naipaul"), father of V. S. Naipaul, and the inspiration for the protagonist of the novel, Mr Biswas, with his [Ford Prefect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Prefect_(car) "Ford Prefect (car)")

Not long after Naipaul began writing _A House for Mr Biswas_, he and Pat moved across town from their attic flat in [Muswell Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muswell_Hill "Muswell Hill") to an upstairs flat in [Streatham Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streatham "Streatham").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008184-59) It was the first home in which they felt comfortable.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008184-59) In his foreword to the 1983 [Alfred A. Knopf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_A._Knopf "Alfred A. Knopf") edition of the book, Naipaul was to write:

> "I had more than changed flats: for the first time in my life I enjoyed solitude and freedom in a house. And just as, in the novel, I was able to let myself go, so in the solitude of the quiet, friendly house in Streatham Hill I could let myself go. ... The two years spent on this novel in Streatham Hill remain the most consuming, the most fulfilled, the happiest years of my life. They were my Eden."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1983a133,_136-60)

The book is an imagined version of his father's life as fashioned from childhood memories.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008192-61) The story as it evolved became so real for Naipaul, that he later claimed it had "destroyed memory" in some respects.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008192-61) The protagonist, Mohun Biswas, referred to throughout the book as Mr Biswas, is propelled by the forces of circumstance into a succession of vocations: apprentice to a Hindu priest; a signboard painter; a grocery store proprietor in the "heart of the sugarcane area"; a driver, or "sub-overseer," in a dark, damp and overgrown estate; and a reporter for _The Trinidad Sentinel_.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008193-62) What ambition or resourcefulness Mr Biswas possesses is inevitably undermined by his dependence on his powerful in-laws and the vagaries of opportunity in a colonial society.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008193-62) His in-laws, the Tulsis, with whom he lives much of the time, are a large [extended family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_family "Extended family"), and are caricatured with great humour, and some unkindness, in the novel.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008193-62) There is a melancholic streak in Mr Biswas which makes him at times both purposeless and clumsy, but it also stirs flashes of anger and of sniping wit.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008194-63) Humour underpins the many tense relationships in the book.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008194-63) Eventually, as times change, as two of his children go abroad for college, and as ill health overcomes him, he buys a house, with money borrowed from a friend, and moves into it with his wife and remaining children, and in small measure strikes out on his own before he dies at age 46.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008194-63) According to the author [Patrick French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_French "Patrick French"), _A House for Mr Biswas_ is "universal in the way that the work of Dickens or Tolstoy is universal; the book makes no apologies for itself, and does not contextualize or exoticize its characters. It reveals a complete world."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008193-62)

The writing of the book consumed Naipaul. In 1983, he would write:

> The book took three years to write. It felt like a career; and there was a short period, towards the end of the writing, when I do believe I knew all or much of the book by heart. The labour ended; the book began to recede. And I found that I was unwilling to re-enter the world I had created, unwilling to expose myself again to the emotions that lay below the comedy. I became nervous of the book. I haven't read it since I passed the proofs in May 1961.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1983a128-64)

The reviews of the book both in the British press and the Caribbean were generous.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008196-65) In _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_, Colin McInnes wrote that the book had the "unforced pace of a masterpiece: it is relaxed, yet on every page alert".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008196-65) Francis Wyndham, writing in the _[London Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London\_Magazine "London Magazine")_, suggested that the book was "one of the clearest and subtlest illustrations ever shown of the effects of colonialism ...."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008196-65) In his _Trinidad Guardian_ review, Derek Walcott, judged Naipaul to be "one of the most mature of West Indian writers".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008196-65)

In 2011, on the fiftieth anniversary of the publication of _A House for Mr Biswas_, and ten years after Naipaul had won the Nobel Prize in Literature, he dedicated the book to his late wife Patricia Anne Hale, who had died in 1996.

### 1961–1963: _The Middle Passage_, India, _An Area of Darkness_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 1961–1963: The Middle Passage, India, An Area of Darkness")]

*   [![Image 13: Eric Williams, the Premier of Trinidad and Tobago, invited Naipaul to visit in early 1961 and to write a book on Caribbean history, published as The Middle Passage.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0c/Eric_Williams_Trinidad_Independence.jpg/250px-Eric_Williams_Trinidad_Independence.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eric_Williams_Trinidad_Independence.jpg "Eric Williams, the Premier of Trinidad and Tobago, invited Naipaul to visit in early 1961 and to write a book on Caribbean history, published as The Middle Passage.") [Eric Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Williams "Eric Williams"), the [Premier of Trinidad and Tobago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Prime_Ministers_of_Trinidad_and_Tobago#Premier_of_Trinidad_and_Tobago_.281959.E2.80.9362.29 "List of Prime Ministers of Trinidad and Tobago"), invited Naipaul to visit in early 1961 and to write a book on Caribbean history, published as _[The Middle Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Middle\_Passage\_(book) "The Middle Passage (book)")_. 
*   [![Image 14: Naipaul wrote a monthly "Letter from London" for the Illustrated Weekly of India from 1963 to 1965.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Illustrated_Weekly_of_India_January_1947.JPG/250px-Illustrated_Weekly_of_India_January_1947.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illustrated_Weekly_of_India_January_1947.JPG "Naipaul wrote a monthly \"Letter from London\" for the Illustrated Weekly of India from 1963 to 1965.") Naipaul wrote a monthly "Letter from London" for the _[Illustrated Weekly of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrated\_Weekly\_of\_India "Illustrated Weekly of India")_ from 1963 to 1965. 

In September 1960, Naipaul was sounded out about visiting Trinidad as a guest of the government and giving a few lectures.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008201-66) The following month an invitation arrived offering an all-expenses-paid trip and a stipend.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008201-66) Naipaul and Pat, both exhausted after the completion of _A House for Mr Biswas_, spent the next five months in the Caribbean.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008201-66) In Port of Spain, Naipaul was invited by [Eric Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Williams "Eric Williams"), [Premier of Trinidad and Tobago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Prime_Ministers_of_Trinidad_and_Tobago#Premier_of_Trinidad_and_Tobago_.281959.E2.80.9362.29 "List of Prime Ministers of Trinidad and Tobago") within the short-lived [West Indies Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies_Federation "West Indies Federation"), to visit other countries of the region and write a book on the Caribbean.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008201%E2%80%93202-67)_[The Middle Passage: Impressions of Five Societies – British, French and Dutch in the West Indies and South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Middle\_Passage\_(book) "The Middle Passage (book)")_, Naipaul's first work of travel writing, was the result.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008201-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200637-68) To gather material for the book, Naipaul and Pat travelled to [British Guiana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Guiana "British Guiana"), Suriname, Martinique and [Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colony_of_Jamaica "Colony of Jamaica").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200637-68)

The book begins with perceptive, lively, but unflattering and gratuitously descriptive portraits of fellow passengers bound for Trinidad.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200637%E2%80%9338-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008202-70) Although he was later criticised for the insensitiveness of these descriptions, he stood by his book, claiming it was "a very funny book",[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200637%E2%80%9338-69) and that he was employing a form of irreverent West Indian humour.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008202-70) Naipaul does not attempt to be detached in the book, continually reminding the reader of his own ties to the region.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200639-71) For him, the West Indies are islands colonised only for the purpose of employing slaves for the production of other people's goods; he states, "The history of the islands can never be told satisfactorily. Brutality is not the only difficulty. History is built around achievement and creation; and nothing was created in the [West Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indies "West Indies")."[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008203-72) As the narrative progresses, Naipaul becomes more sympathetic and insightful, noting that no African names remain on the islands; that slavery had engendered "self-contempt," impelling the descendants of the slaves to idealise European civilisation and to look down on all others; and that the debasement of identity has created racial animosity and rivalry among the brutalised peoples.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008203-72) As Naipaul does not see nationalism as having taken root in these societies, only cults of personality, he does not celebrate the coming of independence, though he does not suggest a return to colonial subjecthood.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008203-72)

In early 1962, Naipaul and Pat arrived in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") for a year-long visit. It was Naipaul's first visit to the land of his ancestors. The title of the resulting book, _[An Area of Darkness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/An\_Area\_of\_Darkness "An Area of Darkness")_, was not so much a reference to India as to Naipaul's effort to understand India.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008230-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200644-74) Soon after arrival, Naipaul was overwhelmed by two sensations. First, for the first time in his life, he felt anonymous, even faceless. He was no longer identified, he felt, as part of a special ethnic group as he had been in Trinidad or England and this made him anxious.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008215-75)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200641%E2%80%9342-76) Second, he was upset by what he saw was the resigned or evasive Indian reaction to poverty and suffering.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008217-77)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200642%E2%80%9343-78) After a month in [Bombay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai") and [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi"), Naipaul and Pat spent five months in [Jammu and Kashmir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jammu_and_Kashmir_(state) "Jammu and Kashmir (state)"), staying in the lakeside Hotel Liward in [Srinagar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Srinagar "Srinagar").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200643%E2%80%9344-79) Here, Naipaul wrote a novella, _Mr Stone and the Knights Companion_, set in London, and based, in part, on his experiences working for the Cement and Concrete Association, and, in part, on his relationship with Pat.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008218%E2%80%93219-80) He wrote a number of short stories which were eventually published in the collection _[A Flag on the Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Flag\_on\_the\_Island "A Flag on the Island")_. His evolving relationship with the hotel manager, Mr. Butt, and especially his assistant, Mr. Aziz, became the subject of the middle section of _An Area of Darkness_, Naipaul bringing his novelistic skills and economy of style to bear with good effect.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200643%E2%80%9344-79) During the rest of his stay, his frustration with some aspects of India mounted even as he felt an attraction to other aspects.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008226%E2%80%93227-81)[Gorakhpur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorakhpur "Gorakhpur"), in eastern [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh"), he wrote later, had "reduced him to the early-Indian stage of (his) hysteria".[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008226%E2%80%93227-81) During his visit to his ancestral village, soon afterwards, Naipaul impatiently turned down a request for assistance and made a quick escape.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008226%E2%80%93227-81) But in a letter, he also wrote: "As you can imagine I fell in love with these beautiful people, their so beautiful women who have all the boldness and independence ... of [Brahmin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brahmin "Brahmin") women ... and their enchanting fairy-tale village."[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008226%E2%80%93227-81)

Just before he left India, Naipaul was invited by the editor of the _[Illustrated Weekly of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illustrated\_Weekly\_of\_India "Illustrated Weekly of India")_, a prominent, established, English-language magazine, to write a monthly "Letter from London" for the magazine.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008232%E2%80%93233-82) Naipaul accepted for a fee of [£](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pound_sign "Pound sign")30 a letter.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008232%E2%80%93233-82) He wrote a monthly letter for the next two years.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008232%E2%80%93233-82) It would be the only time he would write regularly on the contemporary culture in England, his country of domicile.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008232%E2%80%93233-82) The topics included [cricket](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cricket "Cricket"), [The Beatles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Beatles "The Beatles"), the [Profumo affair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Profumo_affair "Profumo affair"), advertising in the [London Tube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Underground "London Underground"), and the Queen.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008232%E2%80%93233-82)

### 1964–1967: _A Flag on the Island_, Africa, _The Mimic Men_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=V._S._Naipaul&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 1964–1967: A Flag on the Island, Africa, The Mimic Men")]

See also: [A Flag on the Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Flag_on_the_Island "A Flag on the Island") and [The Mimic Men](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Mimic_Men "The Mimic Men")

*   [![Image 15: A beach near Scarborough, Tobago, similar to the one on the fictional island of Isabella in The Mimic Men.](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Beach%2C_Scarborough%2C_Tobago%2C_1947.jpg/250px-Beach%2C_Scarborough%2C_Tobago%2C_1947.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Beach,_Scarborough,_Tobago,_1947.jpg "A beach near Scarborough, Tobago, similar to the one on the fictional island of Isabella in The Mimic Men.") A beach near Scarborough, [Tobago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tobago "Tobago"), similar to the one on the fictional island of Isabella in _The Mimic Men_. 
*   [![Image 16: Naipaul served as writer-in-residence at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, and finished his novel The Mimic Men](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Makerere_University_tower.jpg/250px-Makerere_University_tower.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Makerere_University_tower.jpg "Naipaul served as writer-in-residence at Makerere University in Kampala, Uganda, and finished his novel The Mimic Men") Naipaul served as writer-in-residence at [Makerere University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makerere_University "Makerere University") in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"), Uganda, and finished his novel _The Mimic Men_ 

> "Coconut trees and beach and the white of breakers seemed to meet at a point in the distance. It was not possible to see where coconut turned to mangrove and swampland. Here and there, interrupting the straight line of the beach, were the trunks of trees washed up by the sea. I set myself to walk to one tree, then to the other. I was soon far away from the village and from people, and was alone on the beach, smooth and shining silver in the dying light. No coconut now, but mangrove, tall on the black cages of their roots. From the mangrove swamps channels ran to the ocean between sand banks that were daily made and broken off, as neatly as if cut by machines, shallow channels of clear water touched with the amber of dead leaves, cool to the feet, different from the warm sea."

—From, _The Mimic Men_ (1967).[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTENaipaul1967133-83)

Naipaul had spent an overwrought year in India.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008239-84) Back in London, after _An Area of Darkness_ was completed, he felt creatively drained.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008239-84) He felt he had used up his Trinidad material.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008219%E2%80%93220-85) Neither India nor the writing of _Mr Stone and the Knights Companion_, his only attempt at a novel set in Britain with white British characters, had spurred new ideas for imaginative writing.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008219%E2%80%93220-85) His finances too were low, and Pat went back to teaching to supplement them.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008239-84) Naipaul's books had received much critical acclaim, but they were not yet money makers.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008239-84) Socially, he was now breaking away from the _Caribbean Voices_ circle, but no doors had opened to mainstream British society.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008240-86)

That changed when Naipaul was introduced to [Antonia Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonia_Fraser "Antonia Fraser"), at the time the wife of conservative politician [Hugh Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Fraser_(British_politician) "Hugh Fraser (British politician)").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008241%E2%80%93242-87) Fraser introduced Naipaul to her social circle of upper-class British politicians, writers, and performing artists.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008241%E2%80%93242-87) In this circle was the wealthy [second Baron Glenconner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_Glenconner#Barons_Glenconner_.281911.29 "Baron Glenconner"), father of novelist [Emma Tennant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emma_Tennant "Emma Tennant") and owner of estates in Trinidad, who arranged for an unsecured loan of £7,200 for Naipaul.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008243%E2%80%93244-88) Naipaul and Pat bought a three-floor house on [Stockwell Park Crescent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockwell "Stockwell").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008244-89)

In late 1964, Naipaul was asked to write an original script for an American movie.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008247-90) He spent the next few months in Trinidad writing the story, a novella named, "A Flag on the Island," later published in the collection, _[A Flag on the Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Flag\_on\_the\_Island "A Flag on the Island")_. The finished version was not to the director's liking and the movie was never made.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008247-90) The story is set in the present time—1964—in a Caribbean island, which is not named.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200369-91) The main character is an American named "Frankie" who affects the mannerisms of Frank Sinatra.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008247-90) Frankie has links to the island from having served there during World War II.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200657-92) He revisits reluctantly when his ship anchors there during a hurricane.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200657-92) Naipaul wilfully makes the pace of the book feverish, the narrative haphazard, the characters loud, the protagonist fickle or deceptive, and the dialogue confusing.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200657-92)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008247-90) Balancing the present time is Frankie's less disordered, though comfortless, memory of 20 years before.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200658-93) Then he had become a part of a community on the island.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200658-93) He had tried to help his poor friends by giving away the ample US Army supplies he had.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200658-93) Not everyone was happy about receiving help and not everyone benefited.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200658-93) Frankie was left chastened about finding tidy solutions to the island's social problems.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200658-93) This theme, indirectly developed in the story, is one to which Naipaul would return.

Not long after finishing _[A Flag on the Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A\_Flag\_on\_the\_Island "A Flag on the Island")_, Naipaul began work on the novel _The Mimic Men_, though for almost a year he did not make significant progress.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008248-94) At the end of this period, he was offered a Writer-in-Residence fellowship at [Makerere University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makerere_University "Makerere University") in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala"), Uganda.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008249-95) There, in early 1966, Naipaul began to rewrite his material and went on to complete the novel quickly.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008250-96) The finished novel broke new ground for him.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008250-96) Unlike his Caribbean work, it was not comic.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200655-97) It did not unfold chronologically.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200377%E2%80%9378-98) Its language was allusive and ironic, its overall structure whimsical.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200371-99) It had strands of both fiction and non-fiction, a precursor of other Naipaul novels.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200654-100) It was intermittently dense, even obscure,[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200377%E2%80%9378-98) but it also had beautiful passages, especially descriptive ones of the fictional tropical island of Isabella. The subject of sex appeared explicitly for the first time in Naipaul's work.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDooley200653-101) The plot, to the extent there is one, is centred around a protagonist, Ralph Singh, an [East Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_people "Indian people")-[West Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Indian "West Indian") politician from Isabella.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200371-99) Singh is in exile in London and attempting to write his political memoirs.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200371-99) Earlier, in the immediate aftermath of [decolonisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decolonisation "Decolonisation") in a number of British colonies in the late 1950s and early 1960s, Singh had shared political power with a more powerful African Caribbean politician. Soon, the memoirs take on a more personal aspect. There are flashbacks to the formative and defining periods of Singh's life. In many of these, during crucial moments, whether during his childhood, married life, or political career, he appears to abandon engagement and enterprise.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200371-99) These, he rationalises later, belong only to fully made European societies. When _The Mimic Men_ was published, it received generally positive critical notice. In particular, Caribbean politicians, such as [Michael Manley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Manley "Michael Manley") and [Eric Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Williams "Eric Williams") weighed in, the latter writing, "V. S. Naipaul's description of West Indians as 'mimic men' is harsh but true ..."[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008257-102)

Before Naipaul began writing _The Loss of El Dorado_, he had been unhappy with the political climate in Britain.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008270-105) He had been especially unhappy with the increasing public animosity, in the mid-1960s, towards Asian immigrants from Britain's ex-colonies.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008270-105) During the writing of the book, he and Pat sold their house in London, and led a transient life, successively renting or borrowing use of the homes of friends. As it turned out, _The Loss of El Dorado_ sold only 3,000 copies in the US, where major sales were expected; Naipaul also missed England more than he had calculated. It was thus in a depleted state, both financial and emotional, that he returned to Britain.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200384%E2%80%9385-106)

Earlier, during their time in Africa, Naipaul and Pat had travelled to Kenya, staying for a month in [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa") on the Indian Ocean coast.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008253-107) They had travelled in rural Uganda to [Kisoro District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kisoro_District "Kisoro District") on the south-western border with Rwanda and the Congo.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008253-107) Naipaul showed interest in the clans of the [Bagandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baganda "Baganda") people.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008253-107) When Uganda's prime minister [Milton Obote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milton_Obote "Milton Obote") overthrew their ruler, the [Kabaka of Buganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabaka_of_Buganda "Kabaka of Buganda"), Naipaul was critical of the British press for not condemning [the action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Mengo_Hill "Battle of Mengo Hill") enough.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008254-108) Naipaul also travelled to Tanzania with a young American he had met in Kampala, [Paul Theroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Theroux "Paul Theroux").[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008254-108) It was upon this African experience that Naipaul would draw during the writing of his next book, _[In a Free State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/In\_a\_Free\_State "In a Free State")_.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEFrench2008255-109)

In the title novella, 'In a Free State', at the heart of the book, two young expatriate Europeans drive across an African country, which remains nameless, but offers clues about Uganda, Kenya, and Rwanda.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200391%E2%80%9392-110) The novella speaks to many themes. The colonial era ends and Africans govern themselves.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200391%E2%80%9392-110) Political chaos, frequently violent, takes hold in newly decolonised countries.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200391%E2%80%9392-110) Young, idealistic, expatriate whites are attracted to these countries, seeking expanded moral and sexual freedoms. They are rootless, their bonds with the land tenuous; at the slightest danger they leave.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200387%E2%80%9388-111) The older, conservative, white settlers, by contrast, are committed to staying, even in the face of danger.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200387%E2%80%9388-111) The young expatriates, though liberal, can be racially prejudiced.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200387%E2%80%9388-111) The old settlers, unsentimental, and sometimes brutal, can show compassion.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200388-112) The young, engrossed in narrow preoccupations, are uncomprehending of the dangers that surround them.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200387%E2%80%9388-111) The old are knowledgeable, armed, and ready to defend themselves.[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200388-112) The events unfolding along the car trip and the conversation during it become the means of exploring these themes.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V._S._Naipaul#cite_note-FOOTNOTEKing200387%E2%80%9388-111)
