**Ferit Orhan Pamuk** (born 7 June 1952; Turkish pronunciation:[[feˈɾit oɾˈhan paˈmuk]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Turkish "Help:IPA/Turkish")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-1)) is a Turkish novelist, screenwriter, academic, and recipient of the [2006 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2006 Nobel Prize in Literature"). One of Turkey's most prominent novelists,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Kinzer1998-12-15-2) he has sold over 13 million books in 63 languages,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-3-3) making him the country's best-selling writer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-4-4)

Pamuk's novels include _[Silent House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent\_House\_(novel) "Silent House (novel)")_, _[The White Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_White\_Castle "The White Castle")_, _[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Pamuk novel)")_, _[The New Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Life\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The New Life (Pamuk novel)")_, _[My Name Is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_Is\_Red "My Name Is Red")_ and _[Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow\_(Pamuk\_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")_. He is the Robert Yik-Fong Tam Professor in the Humanities at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), where he teaches [writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing "Writing") and [comparative literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative_literature "Comparative literature"). He was elected to the [American Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Philosophical_Society "American Philosophical Society") in 2018.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-5)

Born in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), Pamuk is the first Turkish Nobel laureate. He has also received many other literary awards. _My Name Is Red_ won the 2002 [Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix_du_Meilleur_Livre_%C3%89tranger "Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger"), the 2002 [Premio Grinzane Cavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premio_Grinzane_Cavour "Premio Grinzane Cavour"), and the 2003 [International Dublin Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dublin_Literary_Award "International Dublin Literary Award").

The European Writers' Parliament came about as a result of a joint proposal by Pamuk and [José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-6) Pamuk's willingness to write books about contentious historical and political events put him at risk of censure in his homeland. In 2005, a lawyer sued him over a statement acknowledging the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") in the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-21-7) Pamuk said his intention had been to highlight issues of [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") in Turkey. The court initially declined to hear the case, but in 2011 Pamuk was ordered to pay 6,000 liras in compensation for having insulted the plaintiffs' honor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hurriyetdailynews1-8)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Pamuk was born in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), in 1952, and grew up in a wealthy but declining upper-class family, an experience he describes in passing in his novels _[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Orhan\_Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Orhan Pamuk novel)")_ and _Cevdet Bey and His Sons_, as well as more thoroughly in his personal memoir _Istanbul: Memories and the City_. Pamuk's paternal grandmother was [Circassian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circassians "Circassians").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-9) He was educated at [Robert College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_College "Robert College") secondary school in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") and studied architecture at the [Istanbul Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Technical_University "Istanbul Technical University"), a subject related to his dream career, painting.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Jaggi2008-12-08-10) He left architecture school after three years to become a full-time writer, and graduated from the Institute of [Journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism "Journalism") at the [University of Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Istanbul "University of Istanbul") in 1976. From ages 22 to 30, Pamuk lived with his mother, writing his first novel and attempting to find a publisher. He describes himself as a [Cultural Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Muslim "Cultural Muslim") who identifies with Islam historically and culturally while not believing in a personal connection to God.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-6-11)

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Orhan_Pamuk.jpg/250px-Orhan_Pamuk.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Orhan_Pamuk.jpg)

Pamuk and his [Turkish Angora cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Angora "Turkish Angora") at his personal writing space

Pamuk started writing regularly in 1974.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-NobelFaces-12) His first novel, _Karanlık ve Işık_ (_Darkness and Light_) was a co-winner of the 1979 Milliyet Press Novel Contest ([Mehmet Eroğlu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmet_Ero%C4%9Flu "Mehmet Eroğlu") was the other winner). This novel was published with the title _Cevdet Bey ve Oğulları_ (_Mr. Cevdet and His Sons_) in 1982 and won the [Orhan Kemal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Kemal "Orhan Kemal") Novel Prize in 1983. It tells the story of three generations of a wealthy Istanbul family living in [Nişantaşı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ni%C5%9Fanta%C5%9F%C4%B1 "Nişantaşı"), the district of Istanbul where Pamuk grew up.

Pamuk won a number of critical prizes for his early work, including the 1984 Madarali Novel Prize for his second novel _Sessiz Ev_ (_[Silent House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent\_House\_(novel) "Silent House (novel)")_) and the 1991 Prix de la Découverte Européenne for its French translation. His historical novel _Beyaz Kale_ (_The White Castle_), published in Turkish in 1985, won the 1990 Independent Award for Foreign Fiction and extended his reputation abroad. On 19 May 1991, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ Book Review wrote, "A new star has risen in the east—Orhan Pamuk."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-13) He started experimenting with postmodern techniques in his novels, a change from his early works' strict naturalism.

Popular success took a bit longer, but his 1990 novel _Kara Kitap_ (_[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Pamuk novel)")_) became one of the most controversial and popular books in [Turkish literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_literature "Turkish literature"), due to its complexity and richness. In 1992, he wrote the screenplay for the movie _Gizli Yüz_ (_Secret Face_), based on _Kara Kitap_ and directed by a prominent Turkish director, [Ömer Kavur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%96mer_Kavur "Ömer Kavur"). Pamuk's fifth novel, _Yeni Hayat_ (_New Life_), caused a sensation in Turkey upon its 1994 publication and became the fastest-selling book in Turkish history. By this time, Pamuk had also become a high-profile figure in Turkey due to his support for Kurdish political rights. In 1995, he was among a group of authors tried for writing essays that criticized Turkey's treatment of the Kurds. In 1999, Pamuk published his book of essays _Öteki Renkler_ (_Other Colors_).

In 2019, the 66-year-old Nobel laureate held an exhibition of his photographs of Istanbul taken from his own balcony, "Balkon: Photos by Orhan Pamuk". It captured the "subtle and ever-changing view of Istanbul" photographed by Pamuk from his balcony using a telephoto lens. Curated by [Gerhard Steidl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Steidl "Gerhard Steidl"), the German publisher of his photo book _Balkon_, the exhibition ran for three months at the Yapı Kredi Culture and Arts building on Istanbul's Istiklal Street. It featured more than 600 colour photos selected from over 8,500 Pamuk took over a five-month period in late 2012 and early 2013, in what the gallery called "a period of intense creativity".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-14)

### _My Name Is Red_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: My Name Is Red")]

Main article: [My Name Is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Name_Is_Red "My Name Is Red")

Pamuk's international reputation continued to increase when he published _Benim Adım Kırmızı_ (_[My Name is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_is\_Red "My Name is Red")_) in 1998. The novel blends mystery, romance, and philosophical puzzles in a setting of 16th-century Istanbul. It opens a window into the reign of [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")[Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan")[Murat III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murat_III "Murat III") in nine snowy winter days of 1591, inviting the reader to experience the tension between East and West from a breathlessly urgent perspective. _My Name Is Red_ has been translated into 24 languages and in 2003 won the [International Dublin Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dublin_Literary_Award "International Dublin Literary Award"), one of the world's most lucrative literary prizes.

Asked what impact winning this last award (currently $127,000) had on his life and work, Pamuk replied:

> Nothing changed in my life since I work all the time. I've spent 30 years writing fiction. For the first 10 years, I worried about money and no one asked how much money I made. The second decade I spent money and no one was asking about that. And I've spent the last 10 years with everyone expecting to hear how I spend the money, which I will not do.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-12-15)

### _Snow_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Snow")]

Main article: [Snow (Pamuk novel)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_(Pamuk_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")

Pamuk followed this with the novel _Kar_, published in 2002 (English translation: _[Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow\_(Pamuk\_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")_, 2004). Set in the border city of [Kars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kars "Kars"), it explores the conflict between Islamism and Westernism in modern Turkey. Snow follows Ka, an expatriate Turkish poet, as he wanders around the snowy [Kars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kars "Kars") and gets caught up in the muddle of aimless Islamists, MPs, headscarf advocates, secularists, and a number of factions who die and kill in the name of highly contradictory ideals. _The New York Times_ listed _Snow_ as one of its Ten Best Books of 2004.

In a conversation with Carol Becker in the [Brooklyn Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Rail "Brooklyn Rail") about creating sympathetic characters in the political novel, Pamuk said:

> I strongly feel that the art of the novel is based on the human capacity, though it’s a limited capacity, to be able to identify with "the other". Only human beings can do this. It requires imagination, a sort of morality, a self-imposed goal of understanding this person who is different from us, which is a rarity.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-16)

### _The Museum of Innocence_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: The Museum of Innocence")]

Main article: [The Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Museum_of_Innocence "The Museum of Innocence")

In May 2007, Pamuk was among the jury members at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") headed by British director [Stephen Frears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Frears "Stephen Frears"). He completed his next novel, _Masumiyet Müzesi_ (_[The Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Museum\_of\_Innocence "The Museum of Innocence")_) in the summer of 2008 - the first novel he published after receiving the 2006 Nobel Prize in Literature.

Pamuk created an actual [Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Museum_of_Innocence_(Museum) "The Museum of Innocence (Museum)"), consisting of everyday objects tied to the narrative, and housed them at an [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") house he purchased.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-9-17) Pamuk collaborated on a documentary "The Innocence of Memories"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-19) that expanded on his Museum of Innocence. Pamuk stated that "(Museum of Dreams will) tell a different version of the love story set in Istanbul through objects and Grant Gee’s wonderful new film".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-20) In both _Snow_ and the _Museum of Innocence_ Pamuk describes tragic love-stories, where men fall in love with beautiful women at first sight. Pamuk's heroes tend to be educated men who fall tragically in love with beauties, but who seem doomed to a decrepit loneliness.

In 2013, Pamuk invited [Grazia Toderi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazia_Toderi "Grazia Toderi"), whose work he admired, to design a work for the Museum of Innocence in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"). Their collaboration culminated in the exhibition _Words and Stars_. _Words and Stars_ opened on 2 April 2017, at the MART (Museo di Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Trento e Rovereto), and which explores "the inclination of man to explore space and innate vocation to question the stars." The show was curated by Gianfranco Maraniello.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-21) It also showed from 4 November 2016 to 29 March 2017 from 5–6 November 2016 at the [Palazzo Madama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Madama,_Turin "Palazzo Madama, Turin"), Piazza Castello, [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), and at _Infini-to, the Planetarium of Turin (Infini.to - Planetario di Torino, Museo dell'Astronomia e dello Spazio)_ by invitation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-22)

In 2026, a series based on the novel _The Museum of Innocence_ was released on Netflix. Pamuk stars as himself, and some scenes were filmed at the Museum of Innocence.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-23)

### Non-fiction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Non-fiction")]

Pamuk published the memoir/travelogue _Istanbul—Hatıralar ve Şehir_ in 2003 (English version, _Istanbul—Memories and the City_, 2005). Pamuk's _Other Colours—_ a collection of nonfiction and a story—was published in the UK in September 2007.

Asked how personal his book _Istanbul: Memories and the City_ was, Pamuk replied:

> I thought I would write _Memories and the City_ in six months, but it took me one year to complete. And I was working twelve hours a day, just reading and working. My life, because of so many things, was in a crisis; I don’t want to go into those details: divorce, father dying, professional problems, problems with this, problems with that, everything was bad. I thought if I were to be weak I would have a depression. But every day I would wake up and have a cold shower and sit down and remember and write, always paying attention to the beauty of the book. Honestly, I may have hurt my mother, my family. My father was dead, but my mother is still alive. But I can’t care about that; I must care about the beauty of the book.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-13-24)

## Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Style")]

Pamuk's books are characterized by a confusion or loss of identity brought on in part by the conflict between Western and Eastern values. They are often disturbing or unsettling, and include complex plots and characters. His works are also redolent with discussion of and fascination with the creative arts, such as literature and painting. Pamuk's work often touches on the deep-rooted tensions between East and West and tradition and modernism/secularism.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-25)

Pamuk speaks about "the angel of inspiration" when he discusses his creativity:

> "I am just listening to an inner music, the mystery of which I don't completely know. And I don't want to know."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-14-26)
> 
> 
> "I am most surprised by those moments when I have felt as if the sentences, dreams, and pages that have made me so ecstatically happy have not come from my own imagination– that another power has found them and generously presented them to me."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-16-27)

A group of writers assert that some parts of Pamuk's works are heavily influenced by the works of other writers, and some chapters are almost totally quoted from other books. Pamuk himself said that his works have been inspired by the writings of rebel poet [Kazi Nazrul Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazi_Nazrul_Islam "Kazi Nazrul Islam")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. One of the writers, nationalist popular historian [Murat Bardakçı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murat_Bardak%C3%A7%C4%B1 "Murat Bardakçı"), accused him of counterfeiting and plagiarism in the _Hurriyet_, a Turkish newspaper.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Hurriyet2002-05-26-28) Another accusation is that Pamuk's novel _The White Castle_ contains exact paragraphs from Fuad Carim's _Kanuni Devrinde İstanbul_ ("Istanbul in the Time of the [Kanuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent "Suleiman the Magnificent")") novel.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-19-29) After a question raised at the 2009 [Boston Book Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Book_Festival "Boston Book Festival") as to whether he wanted to respond to these accusations, Pamuk responded, "No I do not. Next question?".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Gracetopia-30) However, many attributed such accusations to their ignorance about [postmodern literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern_literature "Postmodern literature"), and the literary technique of [intertextuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertextuality "Intertextuality") which Pamuk almost always uses in his novels in full disclosure.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Pamuk's elder brother [Şevket Pamuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Eevket_Pamuk "Şevket Pamuk"), who sometimes appears as a fictionalized character in his works, is a professor of economics internationally recognised for his work in [economic history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history "Economic history") of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), working at [Boğaziçi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bo%C4%9Fazi%C3%A7i_University "Boğaziçi University") in Istanbul. Pamuk also has a younger half-sister, Hümeyra Pamuk, who is a journalist.

On 1 March 1982, Pamuk married historian Aylin Türegün.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-7-31) From 1985 to 1988, while she was a graduate student at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), Pamuk assumed the position of visiting scholar there, using the time to conduct research and write his novel _The Black Book_ at the university's [Butler Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_Library "Butler Library"). This period also included a [visiting fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Writing_Program "International Writing Program") at the [University of Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Iowa "University of Iowa"). Pamuk returned to Istanbul, a city to which he is strongly attached.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-8-32) In 1991 he and his wife had a daughter, Rüya, whose name means "dream" in Turkish, and to whom his novel _[My Name is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_is\_Red "My Name is Red")_ is dedicated. In 2002, they were divorced.

In 2006, Pamuk returned to the U.S. to take a position as a visiting professor at Columbia, where he was a Fellow with Columbia's Committee on Global Thought and held an appointment in Columbia's Middle East and Asian Languages and Cultures department and at its [School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_the_Arts "Columbia University School of the Arts"). In the 2007–08 academic year Pamuk returned to Columbia to jointly teach comparative literature classes with [Andreas Huyssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Huyssen "Andreas Huyssen") and David Damrosch. Pamuk was also a writer-in-residence at [Bard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bard_College "Bard College"). In 2009, he was [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")'s [Charles Eliot Norton Lecturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Eliot_Norton_Lectures "Charles Eliot Norton Lectures"), delivering a series of lectures titled "The Naive and Sentimental Novelist".

Orhan publicly acknowledged his relationship with the writer [Kiran Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiran_Desai "Kiran Desai").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-33) In January 2011, Turkish-Armenian artist Karolin Fişekçi told _[Hürriyet Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%BCrriyet\_Daily\_News "Hürriyet Daily News")_ that Pamuk had a two-and-a-half-year relationship with her during the same time (2010–12),[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-34) which Pamuk expressly denied.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-35)

Since 2011 he has been in a relationship with Aslı Akyavaş,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-37) whom he married in 2022.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-38)

[José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago"), [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Garc%C3%ADa_M%C3%A1rquez "Gabriel García Márquez"), [Günter Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Grass "Günter Grass"), [Umberto Eco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco "Umberto Eco"), [Carlos Fuentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Fuentes "Carlos Fuentes"), [Juan Goytisolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Goytisolo "Juan Goytisolo"), [John Updike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Updike "John Updike") and [Mario Vargas Llosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Vargas_Llosa "Mario Vargas Llosa") issued a joint statement in support of Pamuk when he was put on trial in Turkey.

In 2005, after Pamuk made a statement about the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") and mass killings of [Kurds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurdish_people "Kurdish people"), a criminal case was opened against him based on a complaint filed by lawyer [Kemal Kerinçsiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemal_Kerin%C3%A7siz "Kemal Kerinçsiz").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-21-7) The charges were dropped on 22 January 2006. In [Bilecik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilecik "Bilecik"), his books were burned in a nationalist rally.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-22-39) Pamuk subsequently said his intent was to draw attention to [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") issues. Kerinçsiz appealed to the Supreme Court of Appeal, which ordered the court in Şişli to reopen the case. On 27 March 2011, Pamuk was found guilty and ordered to pay 6,000 liras in compensation to five people for, among other things, having insulted their honour.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hurriyetdailynews1-8)

### Pamuk's statements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Pamuk's statements")]

The criminal charges against Pamuk resulted from remarks he made during an interview in February 2005 with the Swiss publication _[Das Magazin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das\_Magazin "Das Magazin")_, a weekly supplement to a number of Swiss daily newspapers: the _[Tages-Anzeiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tages-Anzeiger "Tages-Anzeiger")_, the _[Basler Zeitung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basler\_Zeitung "Basler Zeitung")_, the _[Berner Zeitung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berner\_Zeitung "Berner Zeitung")_ and the _[Solothurner Tagblatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solothurner\_Tagblatt "Solothurner Tagblatt")._ In the interview, Pamuk said, "Thirty thousand Kurds have been killed here, and a million Armenians. And almost nobody dares to mention that. So I do."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Peuwsen2005-02-05-40) Turkish historians were divided over the remarks.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Urus2005-02-10-41)

Pamuk said he was consequently subjected to a hate campaign that forced him to flee the country.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Rainsford2005-12-14-42) He returned later in 2005 to face the charges against him. In an interview with _BBC News_, he said that he wanted to defend [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech"), which was Turkey's only hope for coming to terms with its history: "What happened to the Ottoman Armenians in 1915 was a major thing that was hidden from the Turkish nation; it was a taboo. But we have to be able to talk about the past."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Rainsford2005-12-14-42) But when CNN TURK asked Pamuk about his speech, he admitted that he said that "Armenians were killed" but he denied that he said "Turks killed Armenians", and estimated the number of deaths as 1 million in that speech.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Haberpan2005-10-16-43)

### Prosecution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Prosecution")]

At the time, [Article 301](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_301 "Article 301") of the Turkish Penal Code stated: "A person who publicly insults the Republic or Turkish Grand National Assembly, shall be punishable by imprisonment of between six months to three years." Pamuk was charged with violating this law in the interview. In October, after the prosecution had begun, Pamuk reiterated his views in a speech given during an award ceremony in Germany: "I repeat, I said loud and clear that one million Armenians and 30,000 Kurds were killed in Turkey."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-10-23-44)

Article 301's old form before 2005 (and also the new form after the amendments in 2008) required that prosecution under the article needs to be approved by the Ministry of Justice. A few minutes after Pamuk's trial started on 16 December, the judge found that this approval had not yet been received and suspended the proceedings. In an interview published in the _Akşam_ newspaper the same day, then Justice Minister [Cemil Çiçek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemil_%C3%87i%C3%A7ek "Cemil Çiçek") said he had not yet received Pamuk's file but would study it thoroughly once it came.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-12-16-45)

On 29 December 2005, Turkish state prosecutors dropped the charge that Pamuk insulted Turkey's armed forces, although the charge of "insulting Turkishness" remained.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-12-29-46)

### International reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: International reaction")]

The charges against Pamuk caused an international outcry and led to questions in some circles about Turkey's proposed entry into the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"). On 30 November, the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") announced that it would send a delegation of five MEPs led by [Camiel Eurlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camiel_Eurlings "Camiel Eurlings"), to observe the trial.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-26-47) EU Enlargement Commissioner [Olli Rehn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olli_Rehn "Olli Rehn") subsequently stated that the Pamuk case would be a "[litmus test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litmus_test_(politics) "Litmus test (politics)")" of Turkey's commitment to the EU's membership criteria.

On 15 November, British members of parliament criticised the charges against Pamuk.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-48)

On 1 December, [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") released a statement calling for Article 301 to be repealed and for Pamuk and six other people awaiting trial under the act to be freed.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AmnestyUSA301-49)[PEN American Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN_American_Center "PEN American Center") also denounced the charges against Pamuk, stating: "PEN finds it extraordinary that a state that has ratified both the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations")[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Covenant_on_Civil_and_Political_Rights "International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights"), and the [European Convention on Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights "European Convention on Human Rights"), both of which see freedom of expression as central, should have a Penal Code that includes a clause that is so clearly contrary to these very same principles."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-28-50)

On 13 December, eight world-renowned authors—[José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago"), [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Garc%C3%ADa_M%C3%A1rquez "Gabriel García Márquez"), [Günter Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Grass "Günter Grass"), [Umberto Eco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco "Umberto Eco"), [Carlos Fuentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Fuentes "Carlos Fuentes"), [Juan Goytisolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Goytisolo "Juan Goytisolo"), [John Updike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Updike "John Updike") and [Mario Vargas Llosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Vargas_Llosa "Mario Vargas Llosa")—issued a joint statement supporting Pamuk and decrying the charges against him as a violation of [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-29-51)

In 2008, in an open online poll, Pamuk was voted as the fourth most intellectual person in the world on the list of Top 100 Public Intellectuals by _[Prospect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospect\_(magazine) "Prospect (magazine)")_ (United Kingdom) and _[Foreign Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign\_Policy\_(magazine) "Foreign Policy (magazine)")_ (United States).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-52)

### Charges dropped

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Charges dropped")]

On 22 January 2006, Turkey's Justice Ministry refused to issue an approval of the prosecution, saying that they had no authority to open a case against Pamuk under the new penal code.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Murat-53) With the trial in the local court, it was ruled the next day that the case could not continue without Justice Ministry approval.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Selcan2006-01-23-54) Pamuk's lawyer, Haluk İnanıcı, subsequently confirmed that the charges had been dropped.

The announcement occurred in a week when the EU was scheduled to begin a review of the Turkish justice system.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Selcan2006-01-23-54)

### Interplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Interplay")]

EU enlargement commissioner [Olli Rehn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olli_Rehn "Olli Rehn") welcomed the dropping of charges, saying, "This is obviously good news for Mr. Pamuk, but it's also good news for freedom of expression in Turkey".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Times2006-01-23-55) But some EU representatives expressed disappointment that the justice ministry had rejected the prosecution on a technicality rather than on principle. An Ankara-based EU diplomat reportedly said, "It is good the case has apparently been dropped, but the justice ministry never took a clear position or gave any sign of trying to defend Pamuk".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Ersoy2006-01-22-56) Meanwhile, the lawyer who had led the effort to try Pamuk, Kemal Kerinçsiz, said he would appeal the decision, saying, "Orhan Pamuk must be punished for insulting Turkey and Turkishness, it is a grave crime and it should not be left unpunished."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Times2006-01-23-55)

In 2006, the magazine _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ listed Pamuk in the cover article "TIME 100: The People Who Shape Our World", in the category "Heroes & Pioneers", for speaking up.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Chua-Eoan2006-57)

In April 2006, on the BBC's _[HARDtalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HARDtalk "HARDtalk")_ program, Pamuk stated that his remarks regarding the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") were meant to draw attention to freedom of expression issues in Turkey rather than to the massacres themselves.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hardtalk-58)

On 19–20 December 2006, a symposium on _Orhan Pamuk and His Work_ was held at [Sabancı University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabanc%C4%B1_University "Sabancı University"), Istanbul. Pamuk himself gave the closing address.

In January 2008, Turkish authorities arrested 13 ultranationalists, including Kerinçsiz, for participating in a Turkish nationalist underground organisation, _[Ergenekon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergenekon\_(organization) "Ergenekon (organization)")_, allegedly conspiring to assassinate political figures, including several Christian missionaries and Armenian intellectual [Hrant Dink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hrant_Dink "Hrant Dink").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-33-59) Several reports suggest that Pamuk was among the figures this group plotted to kill.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-34-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Lea2008-01-28-62) The police informed Pamuk about the assassination plans eight months before the Ergenekon investigation.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-36-63)

**Ferit Orhan Pamuk** (born 7 June 1952; Turkish pronunciation:[[feˈɾit oɾˈhan paˈmuk]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Turkish "Help:IPA/Turkish")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-1)) is a Turkish novelist, screenwriter, academic, and recipient of the [2006 Nobel Prize in Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Nobel_Prize_in_Literature "2006 Nobel Prize in Literature"). One of Turkey's most prominent novelists,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Kinzer1998-12-15-2) he has sold over 13 million books in 63 languages,[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-3-3) making him the country's best-selling writer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-4-4)

Pamuk's novels include _[Silent House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent\_House\_(novel) "Silent House (novel)")_, _[The White Castle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_White\_Castle "The White Castle")_, _[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Pamuk novel)")_, _[The New Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Life\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The New Life (Pamuk novel)")_, _[My Name Is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_Is\_Red "My Name Is Red")_ and _[Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow\_(Pamuk\_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")_. He is the Robert Yik-Fong Tam Professor in the Humanities at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), where he teaches [writing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writing "Writing") and [comparative literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparative_literature "Comparative literature"). He was elected to the [American Philosophical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Philosophical_Society "American Philosophical Society") in 2018.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-5)

Born in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), Pamuk is the first Turkish Nobel laureate. He has also received many other literary awards. _My Name Is Red_ won the 2002 [Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prix_du_Meilleur_Livre_%C3%89tranger "Prix du Meilleur Livre Étranger"), the 2002 [Premio Grinzane Cavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premio_Grinzane_Cavour "Premio Grinzane Cavour"), and the 2003 [International Dublin Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dublin_Literary_Award "International Dublin Literary Award").

The European Writers' Parliament came about as a result of a joint proposal by Pamuk and [José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-6) Pamuk's willingness to write books about contentious historical and political events put him at risk of censure in his homeland. In 2005, a lawyer sued him over a statement acknowledging the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") in the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-21-7) Pamuk said his intention had been to highlight issues of [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") in Turkey. The court initially declined to hear the case, but in 2011 Pamuk was ordered to pay 6,000 liras in compensation for having insulted the plaintiffs' honor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hurriyetdailynews1-8)

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Pamuk was born in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"), in 1952, and grew up in a wealthy but declining upper-class family, an experience he describes in passing in his novels _[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Orhan\_Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Orhan Pamuk novel)")_ and _Cevdet Bey and His Sons_, as well as more thoroughly in his personal memoir _Istanbul: Memories and the City_. Pamuk's paternal grandmother was [Circassian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circassians "Circassians").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-9) He was educated at [Robert College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_College "Robert College") secondary school in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") and studied architecture at the [Istanbul Technical University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul_Technical_University "Istanbul Technical University"), a subject related to his dream career, painting.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Jaggi2008-12-08-10) He left architecture school after three years to become a full-time writer, and graduated from the Institute of [Journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism "Journalism") at the [University of Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Istanbul "University of Istanbul") in 1976. From ages 22 to 30, Pamuk lived with his mother, writing his first novel and attempting to find a publisher. He describes himself as a [Cultural Muslim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Muslim "Cultural Muslim") who identifies with Islam historically and culturally while not believing in a personal connection to God.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-6-11)

## Work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Work")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Orhan_Pamuk.jpg/250px-Orhan_Pamuk.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Orhan_Pamuk.jpg)

Pamuk and his [Turkish Angora cat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_Angora "Turkish Angora") at his personal writing space

Pamuk started writing regularly in 1974.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-NobelFaces-12) His first novel, _Karanlık ve Işık_ (_Darkness and Light_) was a co-winner of the 1979 Milliyet Press Novel Contest ([Mehmet Eroğlu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mehmet_Ero%C4%9Flu "Mehmet Eroğlu") was the other winner). This novel was published with the title _Cevdet Bey ve Oğulları_ (_Mr. Cevdet and His Sons_) in 1982 and won the [Orhan Kemal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Kemal "Orhan Kemal") Novel Prize in 1983. It tells the story of three generations of a wealthy Istanbul family living in [Nişantaşı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ni%C5%9Fanta%C5%9F%C4%B1 "Nişantaşı"), the district of Istanbul where Pamuk grew up.

Pamuk won a number of critical prizes for his early work, including the 1984 Madarali Novel Prize for his second novel _Sessiz Ev_ (_[Silent House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silent\_House\_(novel) "Silent House (novel)")_) and the 1991 Prix de la Découverte Européenne for its French translation. His historical novel _Beyaz Kale_ (_The White Castle_), published in Turkish in 1985, won the 1990 Independent Award for Foreign Fiction and extended his reputation abroad. On 19 May 1991, _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ Book Review wrote, "A new star has risen in the east—Orhan Pamuk."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-13) He started experimenting with postmodern techniques in his novels, a change from his early works' strict naturalism.

Popular success took a bit longer, but his 1990 novel _Kara Kitap_ (_[The Black Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Black\_Book\_(Pamuk\_novel) "The Black Book (Pamuk novel)")_) became one of the most controversial and popular books in [Turkish literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_literature "Turkish literature"), due to its complexity and richness. In 1992, he wrote the screenplay for the movie _Gizli Yüz_ (_Secret Face_), based on _Kara Kitap_ and directed by a prominent Turkish director, [Ömer Kavur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%96mer_Kavur "Ömer Kavur"). Pamuk's fifth novel, _Yeni Hayat_ (_New Life_), caused a sensation in Turkey upon its 1994 publication and became the fastest-selling book in Turkish history. By this time, Pamuk had also become a high-profile figure in Turkey due to his support for Kurdish political rights. In 1995, he was among a group of authors tried for writing essays that criticized Turkey's treatment of the Kurds. In 1999, Pamuk published his book of essays _Öteki Renkler_ (_Other Colors_).

In 2019, the 66-year-old Nobel laureate held an exhibition of his photographs of Istanbul taken from his own balcony, "Balkon: Photos by Orhan Pamuk". It captured the "subtle and ever-changing view of Istanbul" photographed by Pamuk from his balcony using a telephoto lens. Curated by [Gerhard Steidl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerhard_Steidl "Gerhard Steidl"), the German publisher of his photo book _Balkon_, the exhibition ran for three months at the Yapı Kredi Culture and Arts building on Istanbul's Istiklal Street. It featured more than 600 colour photos selected from over 8,500 Pamuk took over a five-month period in late 2012 and early 2013, in what the gallery called "a period of intense creativity".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-14)

### _My Name Is Red_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: My Name Is Red")]

Main article: [My Name Is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My_Name_Is_Red "My Name Is Red")

Pamuk's international reputation continued to increase when he published _Benim Adım Kırmızı_ (_[My Name is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_is\_Red "My Name is Red")_) in 1998. The novel blends mystery, romance, and philosophical puzzles in a setting of 16th-century Istanbul. It opens a window into the reign of [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire")[Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan")[Murat III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murat_III "Murat III") in nine snowy winter days of 1591, inviting the reader to experience the tension between East and West from a breathlessly urgent perspective. _My Name Is Red_ has been translated into 24 languages and in 2003 won the [International Dublin Literary Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Dublin_Literary_Award "International Dublin Literary Award"), one of the world's most lucrative literary prizes.

Asked what impact winning this last award (currently $127,000) had on his life and work, Pamuk replied:

> Nothing changed in my life since I work all the time. I've spent 30 years writing fiction. For the first 10 years, I worried about money and no one asked how much money I made. The second decade I spent money and no one was asking about that. And I've spent the last 10 years with everyone expecting to hear how I spend the money, which I will not do.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-12-15)

### _Snow_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Snow")]

Main article: [Snow (Pamuk novel)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow_(Pamuk_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")

Pamuk followed this with the novel _Kar_, published in 2002 (English translation: _[Snow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snow\_(Pamuk\_novel) "Snow (Pamuk novel)")_, 2004). Set in the border city of [Kars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kars "Kars"), it explores the conflict between Islamism and Westernism in modern Turkey. Snow follows Ka, an expatriate Turkish poet, as he wanders around the snowy [Kars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kars "Kars") and gets caught up in the muddle of aimless Islamists, MPs, headscarf advocates, secularists, and a number of factions who die and kill in the name of highly contradictory ideals. _The New York Times_ listed _Snow_ as one of its Ten Best Books of 2004.

In a conversation with Carol Becker in the [Brooklyn Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Rail "Brooklyn Rail") about creating sympathetic characters in the political novel, Pamuk said:

> I strongly feel that the art of the novel is based on the human capacity, though it’s a limited capacity, to be able to identify with "the other". Only human beings can do this. It requires imagination, a sort of morality, a self-imposed goal of understanding this person who is different from us, which is a rarity.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-16)

### _The Museum of Innocence_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: The Museum of Innocence")]

Main article: [The Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Museum_of_Innocence "The Museum of Innocence")

In May 2007, Pamuk was among the jury members at the [Cannes Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes_Film_Festival "Cannes Film Festival") headed by British director [Stephen Frears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephen_Frears "Stephen Frears"). He completed his next novel, _Masumiyet Müzesi_ (_[The Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Museum\_of\_Innocence "The Museum of Innocence")_) in the summer of 2008 - the first novel he published after receiving the 2006 Nobel Prize in Literature.

Pamuk created an actual [Museum of Innocence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Museum_of_Innocence_(Museum) "The Museum of Innocence (Museum)"), consisting of everyday objects tied to the narrative, and housed them at an [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") house he purchased.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-9-17) Pamuk collaborated on a documentary "The Innocence of Memories"[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-19) that expanded on his Museum of Innocence. Pamuk stated that "(Museum of Dreams will) tell a different version of the love story set in Istanbul through objects and Grant Gee’s wonderful new film".[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-20) In both _Snow_ and the _Museum of Innocence_ Pamuk describes tragic love-stories, where men fall in love with beautiful women at first sight. Pamuk's heroes tend to be educated men who fall tragically in love with beauties, but who seem doomed to a decrepit loneliness.

In 2013, Pamuk invited [Grazia Toderi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grazia_Toderi "Grazia Toderi"), whose work he admired, to design a work for the Museum of Innocence in [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"). Their collaboration culminated in the exhibition _Words and Stars_. _Words and Stars_ opened on 2 April 2017, at the MART (Museo di Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Trento e Rovereto), and which explores "the inclination of man to explore space and innate vocation to question the stars." The show was curated by Gianfranco Maraniello.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-21) It also showed from 4 November 2016 to 29 March 2017 from 5–6 November 2016 at the [Palazzo Madama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Madama,_Turin "Palazzo Madama, Turin"), Piazza Castello, [Turin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turin "Turin"), and at _Infini-to, the Planetarium of Turin (Infini.to - Planetario di Torino, Museo dell'Astronomia e dello Spazio)_ by invitation.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-22)

In 2026, a series based on the novel _The Museum of Innocence_ was released on Netflix. Pamuk stars as himself, and some scenes were filmed at the Museum of Innocence.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-23)

### Non-fiction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Non-fiction")]

Pamuk published the memoir/travelogue _Istanbul—Hatıralar ve Şehir_ in 2003 (English version, _Istanbul—Memories and the City_, 2005). Pamuk's _Other Colours—_ a collection of nonfiction and a story—was published in the UK in September 2007.

Asked how personal his book _Istanbul: Memories and the City_ was, Pamuk replied:

> I thought I would write _Memories and the City_ in six months, but it took me one year to complete. And I was working twelve hours a day, just reading and working. My life, because of so many things, was in a crisis; I don’t want to go into those details: divorce, father dying, professional problems, problems with this, problems with that, everything was bad. I thought if I were to be weak I would have a depression. But every day I would wake up and have a cold shower and sit down and remember and write, always paying attention to the beauty of the book. Honestly, I may have hurt my mother, my family. My father was dead, but my mother is still alive. But I can’t care about that; I must care about the beauty of the book.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-13-24)

## Style

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Style")]

Pamuk's books are characterized by a confusion or loss of identity brought on in part by the conflict between Western and Eastern values. They are often disturbing or unsettling, and include complex plots and characters. His works are also redolent with discussion of and fascination with the creative arts, such as literature and painting. Pamuk's work often touches on the deep-rooted tensions between East and West and tradition and modernism/secularism.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-25)

Pamuk speaks about "the angel of inspiration" when he discusses his creativity:

> "I am just listening to an inner music, the mystery of which I don't completely know. And I don't want to know."[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-14-26)
> 
> 
> "I am most surprised by those moments when I have felt as if the sentences, dreams, and pages that have made me so ecstatically happy have not come from my own imagination– that another power has found them and generously presented them to me."[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-16-27)

A group of writers assert that some parts of Pamuk's works are heavily influenced by the works of other writers, and some chapters are almost totally quoted from other books. Pamuk himself said that his works have been inspired by the writings of rebel poet [Kazi Nazrul Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazi_Nazrul_Islam "Kazi Nazrul Islam")[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]. One of the writers, nationalist popular historian [Murat Bardakçı](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murat_Bardak%C3%A7%C4%B1 "Murat Bardakçı"), accused him of counterfeiting and plagiarism in the _Hurriyet_, a Turkish newspaper.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Hurriyet2002-05-26-28) Another accusation is that Pamuk's novel _The White Castle_ contains exact paragraphs from Fuad Carim's _Kanuni Devrinde İstanbul_ ("Istanbul in the Time of the [Kanuni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_the_Magnificent "Suleiman the Magnificent")") novel.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-19-29) After a question raised at the 2009 [Boston Book Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Book_Festival "Boston Book Festival") as to whether he wanted to respond to these accusations, Pamuk responded, "No I do not. Next question?".[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Gracetopia-30) However, many attributed such accusations to their ignorance about [postmodern literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postmodern_literature "Postmodern literature"), and the literary technique of [intertextuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intertextuality "Intertextuality") which Pamuk almost always uses in his novels in full disclosure.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Pamuk's elder brother [Şevket Pamuk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%9Eevket_Pamuk "Şevket Pamuk"), who sometimes appears as a fictionalized character in his works, is a professor of economics internationally recognised for his work in [economic history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history "Economic history") of the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire"), working at [Boğaziçi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bo%C4%9Fazi%C3%A7i_University "Boğaziçi University") in Istanbul. Pamuk also has a younger half-sister, Hümeyra Pamuk, who is a journalist.

On 1 March 1982, Pamuk married historian Aylin Türegün.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-7-31) From 1985 to 1988, while she was a graduate student at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University"), Pamuk assumed the position of visiting scholar there, using the time to conduct research and write his novel _The Black Book_ at the university's [Butler Library](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Butler_Library "Butler Library"). This period also included a [visiting fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Writing_Program "International Writing Program") at the [University of Iowa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Iowa "University of Iowa"). Pamuk returned to Istanbul, a city to which he is strongly attached.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-8-32) In 1991 he and his wife had a daughter, Rüya, whose name means "dream" in Turkish, and to whom his novel _[My Name is Red](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/My\_Name\_is\_Red "My Name is Red")_ is dedicated. In 2002, they were divorced.

In 2006, Pamuk returned to the U.S. to take a position as a visiting professor at Columbia, where he was a Fellow with Columbia's Committee on Global Thought and held an appointment in Columbia's Middle East and Asian Languages and Cultures department and at its [School of the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University_School_of_the_Arts "Columbia University School of the Arts"). In the 2007–08 academic year Pamuk returned to Columbia to jointly teach comparative literature classes with [Andreas Huyssen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andreas_Huyssen "Andreas Huyssen") and David Damrosch. Pamuk was also a writer-in-residence at [Bard College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bard_College "Bard College"). In 2009, he was [Harvard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")'s [Charles Eliot Norton Lecturer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Eliot_Norton_Lectures "Charles Eliot Norton Lectures"), delivering a series of lectures titled "The Naive and Sentimental Novelist".

Orhan publicly acknowledged his relationship with the writer [Kiran Desai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiran_Desai "Kiran Desai").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-33) In January 2011, Turkish-Armenian artist Karolin Fişekçi told _[Hürriyet Daily News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%BCrriyet\_Daily\_News "Hürriyet Daily News")_ that Pamuk had a two-and-a-half-year relationship with her during the same time (2010–12),[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-34) which Pamuk expressly denied.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-35)

Since 2011 he has been in a relationship with Aslı Akyavaş,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-37) whom he married in 2022.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-38)

[José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago"), [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Garc%C3%ADa_M%C3%A1rquez "Gabriel García Márquez"), [Günter Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Grass "Günter Grass"), [Umberto Eco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco "Umberto Eco"), [Carlos Fuentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Fuentes "Carlos Fuentes"), [Juan Goytisolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Goytisolo "Juan Goytisolo"), [John Updike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Updike "John Updike") and [Mario Vargas Llosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Vargas_Llosa "Mario Vargas Llosa") issued a joint statement in support of Pamuk when he was put on trial in Turkey.

In 2005, after Pamuk made a statement about the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") and mass killings of [Kurds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurdish_people "Kurdish people"), a criminal case was opened against him based on a complaint filed by lawyer [Kemal Kerinçsiz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kemal_Kerin%C3%A7siz "Kemal Kerinçsiz").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-21-7) The charges were dropped on 22 January 2006. In [Bilecik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bilecik "Bilecik"), his books were burned in a nationalist rally.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-22-39) Pamuk subsequently said his intent was to draw attention to [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech") issues. Kerinçsiz appealed to the Supreme Court of Appeal, which ordered the court in Şişli to reopen the case. On 27 March 2011, Pamuk was found guilty and ordered to pay 6,000 liras in compensation to five people for, among other things, having insulted their honour.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hurriyetdailynews1-8)

### Pamuk's statements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Pamuk's statements")]

The criminal charges against Pamuk resulted from remarks he made during an interview in February 2005 with the Swiss publication _[Das Magazin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Das\_Magazin "Das Magazin")_, a weekly supplement to a number of Swiss daily newspapers: the _[Tages-Anzeiger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tages-Anzeiger "Tages-Anzeiger")_, the _[Basler Zeitung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basler\_Zeitung "Basler Zeitung")_, the _[Berner Zeitung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berner\_Zeitung "Berner Zeitung")_ and the _[Solothurner Tagblatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solothurner\_Tagblatt "Solothurner Tagblatt")._ In the interview, Pamuk said, "Thirty thousand Kurds have been killed here, and a million Armenians. And almost nobody dares to mention that. So I do."[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Peuwsen2005-02-05-40) Turkish historians were divided over the remarks.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Urus2005-02-10-41)

Pamuk said he was consequently subjected to a hate campaign that forced him to flee the country.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Rainsford2005-12-14-42) He returned later in 2005 to face the charges against him. In an interview with _BBC News_, he said that he wanted to defend [freedom of speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_speech "Freedom of speech"), which was Turkey's only hope for coming to terms with its history: "What happened to the Ottoman Armenians in 1915 was a major thing that was hidden from the Turkish nation; it was a taboo. But we have to be able to talk about the past."[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Rainsford2005-12-14-42) But when CNN TURK asked Pamuk about his speech, he admitted that he said that "Armenians were killed" but he denied that he said "Turks killed Armenians", and estimated the number of deaths as 1 million in that speech.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Haberpan2005-10-16-43)

### Prosecution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Prosecution")]

At the time, [Article 301](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Article_301 "Article 301") of the Turkish Penal Code stated: "A person who publicly insults the Republic or Turkish Grand National Assembly, shall be punishable by imprisonment of between six months to three years." Pamuk was charged with violating this law in the interview. In October, after the prosecution had begun, Pamuk reiterated his views in a speech given during an award ceremony in Germany: "I repeat, I said loud and clear that one million Armenians and 30,000 Kurds were killed in Turkey."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-10-23-44)

Article 301's old form before 2005 (and also the new form after the amendments in 2008) required that prosecution under the article needs to be approved by the Ministry of Justice. A few minutes after Pamuk's trial started on 16 December, the judge found that this approval had not yet been received and suspended the proceedings. In an interview published in the _Akşam_ newspaper the same day, then Justice Minister [Cemil Çiçek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cemil_%C3%87i%C3%A7ek "Cemil Çiçek") said he had not yet received Pamuk's file but would study it thoroughly once it came.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-12-16-45)

On 29 December 2005, Turkish state prosecutors dropped the charge that Pamuk insulted Turkey's armed forces, although the charge of "insulting Turkishness" remained.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-BBC2005-12-29-46)

### International reaction

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: International reaction")]

The charges against Pamuk caused an international outcry and led to questions in some circles about Turkey's proposed entry into the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"). On 30 November, the [European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliament "European Parliament") announced that it would send a delegation of five MEPs led by [Camiel Eurlings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camiel_Eurlings "Camiel Eurlings"), to observe the trial.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-26-47) EU Enlargement Commissioner [Olli Rehn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olli_Rehn "Olli Rehn") subsequently stated that the Pamuk case would be a "[litmus test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litmus_test_(politics) "Litmus test (politics)")" of Turkey's commitment to the EU's membership criteria.

On 15 November, British members of parliament criticised the charges against Pamuk.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-48)

On 1 December, [Amnesty International](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amnesty_International "Amnesty International") released a statement calling for Article 301 to be repealed and for Pamuk and six other people awaiting trial under the act to be freed.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AmnestyUSA301-49)[PEN American Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PEN_American_Center "PEN American Center") also denounced the charges against Pamuk, stating: "PEN finds it extraordinary that a state that has ratified both the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations")[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Covenant_on_Civil_and_Political_Rights "International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights"), and the [European Convention on Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Convention_on_Human_Rights "European Convention on Human Rights"), both of which see freedom of expression as central, should have a Penal Code that includes a clause that is so clearly contrary to these very same principles."[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-28-50)

On 13 December, eight world-renowned authors—[José Saramago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Saramago "José Saramago"), [Gabriel García Márquez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriel_Garc%C3%ADa_M%C3%A1rquez "Gabriel García Márquez"), [Günter Grass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/G%C3%BCnter_Grass "Günter Grass"), [Umberto Eco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Umberto_Eco "Umberto Eco"), [Carlos Fuentes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Fuentes "Carlos Fuentes"), [Juan Goytisolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Goytisolo "Juan Goytisolo"), [John Updike](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Updike "John Updike") and [Mario Vargas Llosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Vargas_Llosa "Mario Vargas Llosa")—issued a joint statement supporting Pamuk and decrying the charges against him as a violation of [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-29-51)

In 2008, in an open online poll, Pamuk was voted as the fourth most intellectual person in the world on the list of Top 100 Public Intellectuals by _[Prospect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prospect\_(magazine) "Prospect (magazine)")_ (United Kingdom) and _[Foreign Policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign\_Policy\_(magazine) "Foreign Policy (magazine)")_ (United States).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-52)

### Charges dropped

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Charges dropped")]

On 22 January 2006, Turkey's Justice Ministry refused to issue an approval of the prosecution, saying that they had no authority to open a case against Pamuk under the new penal code.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Murat-53) With the trial in the local court, it was ruled the next day that the case could not continue without Justice Ministry approval.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Selcan2006-01-23-54) Pamuk's lawyer, Haluk İnanıcı, subsequently confirmed that the charges had been dropped.

The announcement occurred in a week when the EU was scheduled to begin a review of the Turkish justice system.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Selcan2006-01-23-54)

### Interplay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Orhan_Pamuk&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Interplay")]

EU enlargement commissioner [Olli Rehn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olli_Rehn "Olli Rehn") welcomed the dropping of charges, saying, "This is obviously good news for Mr. Pamuk, but it's also good news for freedom of expression in Turkey".[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Times2006-01-23-55) But some EU representatives expressed disappointment that the justice ministry had rejected the prosecution on a technicality rather than on principle. An Ankara-based EU diplomat reportedly said, "It is good the case has apparently been dropped, but the justice ministry never took a clear position or gave any sign of trying to defend Pamuk".[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Ersoy2006-01-22-56) Meanwhile, the lawyer who had led the effort to try Pamuk, Kemal Kerinçsiz, said he would appeal the decision, saying, "Orhan Pamuk must be punished for insulting Turkey and Turkishness, it is a grave crime and it should not be left unpunished."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Times2006-01-23-55)

In 2006, the magazine _[Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_(magazine) "Time (magazine)")_ listed Pamuk in the cover article "TIME 100: The People Who Shape Our World", in the category "Heroes & Pioneers", for speaking up.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Chua-Eoan2006-57)

In April 2006, on the BBC's _[HARDtalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HARDtalk "HARDtalk")_ program, Pamuk stated that his remarks regarding the [Armenian genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_genocide "Armenian genocide") were meant to draw attention to freedom of expression issues in Turkey rather than to the massacres themselves.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-hardtalk-58)

On 19–20 December 2006, a symposium on _Orhan Pamuk and His Work_ was held at [Sabancı University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabanc%C4%B1_University "Sabancı University"), Istanbul. Pamuk himself gave the closing address.

In January 2008, Turkish authorities arrested 13 ultranationalists, including Kerinçsiz, for participating in a Turkish nationalist underground organisation, _[Ergenekon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ergenekon\_(organization) "Ergenekon (organization)")_, allegedly conspiring to assassinate political figures, including several Christian missionaries and Armenian intellectual [Hrant Dink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hrant_Dink "Hrant Dink").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-33-59) Several reports suggest that Pamuk was among the figures this group plotted to kill.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-34-61)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-Lea2008-01-28-62) The police informed Pamuk about the assassination plans eight months before the Ergenekon investigation.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orhan_Pamuk#cite_note-AutoEC-36-63)
